title: Getting Britain Ready: Local resilience, public preparedness and the 'Be Ready' campaign
label: 2 November 2026 · Societal resilience
summary: Witnesses Becky Heginbotham-Blount (Suffolk Chief Resilience Officer, co‑chair of the National Consortium for Societal Resilience) and Professor Lee Miles (Bournemouth University) gave evidence on public awareness of risks, the Government’s three‑year “Be Ready” campaign, the role and funding of local resilience forums, lessons from Covid, the need for education and business engagement, and risks from digital dependence. They agreed the campaign is a useful baseline but said more consistent funding, clearer local communications, incentives for households, and better coordination across government are needed.

glossary.definition: A local partnership of emergency services, councils, NHS and others that plans and coordinates responses to emergencies in a local area.
The UK law setting out how the country prepares for and responds to emergencies.
A public government document listing major risks the country faces, like floods or pandemics.
The Government's three‑year campaign asking households to prepare a basic three‑day emergency kit and steps to be resilient.
Emergency services and other organisations (category 1) and supporting bodies (category 2) that must plan for emergencies.

chapters.title: Public awareness vs household preparedness
chapters.takeaway: Documents and alerts exist, but awareness doesn't always translate into people preparing their households.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The national survey shows 68% expect more emergencies. Are people aware of local risks?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: We publish the National Risk Register and each LRF has a community risk register. People can find the info, but not everyone wants constant detail; the key is trusted, accessible sources.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Risk starts at home. Awareness is different from preparedness: you can know about risks but not act. Messaging is mixed because local hazards and national security threats look different to the public.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The survey says 21% are signed up for flood alerts. Is that realistic?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes—particularly in coastal counties like Suffolk we've pushed flood alerts for years. It's better than nothing, but not high enough.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Twenty‑one percent shows awareness but not enough preparedness. Climate change is increasing frequency of events; the real question is what people do to prepare.

turns.speaker: Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom
turns.text: Do different age groups behave differently?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes. Children focus on fire from school events; older people worry about evacuation and power cuts. Covid also left a mark—some people remain anxious about pandemics.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you see clear stratification by age in preparedness mindsets?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: There are many variables but households' vulnerability and resources matter: many won't invest in preparedness unless they see clear need, and trust in institutions has fallen.

chapters.title: The 'Be Ready' campaign: baseline, not a solution
chapters.takeaway: ‘Be Ready’ is a useful start (three days), but needs follow‑up, incentives, and care given cost‑of‑living pressures.

turns.speaker: Baroness Tyler of Enfield
turns.text: Three days of supplies is familiar, but is that enough and is the campaign sufficient?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Three days is a good baseline and gives consistent messaging across LRFs. Some countries advise longer, and the campaign helps standardise what was previously inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: It’s the start of a journey. We need a mindset shift so households see resilience as partly their responsibility—82% in a survey still think it's the government's job.

turns.speaker: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi
turns.text: Could the cost‑of‑living crisis make the messaging unrealistic? Will people be able to afford preparedness?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Yes—people are rational actors with limited budgets. Incentives matter: discounted preparedness packs, insurance discounts, or business partnerships could help.

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Local experience is mixed: active community groups will engage; many people are overloaded and won't. The National Emergencies Trust's 'Ready Together' helps community groups, which is useful.

turns.speaker: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi
turns.text: Is the campaign being taken seriously or mocked on social media?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Early signs are mixed—some social media jokes—but it's only been two weeks locally. We'll watch how it lands in communities and adapt local outreach.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: The goal is to turn 'Be Ready' into ongoing behaviour—'being ready'—and to back it with financing and business engagement so people can act in practice, not just read checklists.

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Practically, that means clearer local messaging, discount options for lower‑income households, and working with supermarkets and charities to offer affordable preparedness packs.

chapters.title: Local resilience forums: roles, funding and visibility
chapters.takeaway: LRFs coordinate local response well in places with resources, but public awareness, consistent funding and clearer boundaries are lacking.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: Is it clear who does what between central and local government in a crisis?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: LRFs have existed since 2004 and can co‑ordinate well. We learned from Covid to have single standing coordination for concurrent incidents. But capacity varies by area.

turns.speaker: Lord Watts
turns.text: Do first and second responders coordinate with LRFs?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes—category 1 and 2 responders are integrated into planning. Building those relationships in peacetime is essential so systems work in an emergency.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: 73% had never heard of their LRF. Should we run a public campaign to explain what LRFs do and who to contact locally?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: LRFs are part of a wider mesh—households, communities and regional institutions. If LRFs are to be central, they need profile and funding and must not be the sole dependents of local goodwill.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: So, Becky, should LRFs have a recognisable public spokesperson or brand?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes. We're piloting public branding like 'Suffolk Prepared' so partners’ messages are recognisable. That builds trust and helps counter misinformation during incidents.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: One-word: should MPs have a role in local resilience?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes, MPs should be part of local reassurance and communications—people relate to local figures and MPs can help amplify accurate resilience messaging.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Yes—their local authority and visibility gives political accountability and public reach, which helps link national policy and local action in a crisis.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: How was the trailblazer funding decided and is it working?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: LRFs bid with expressions of interest. Five trailblazers were chosen to pilot different approaches; an independent evaluation is underway to see what scales up.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: If the Civil Contingencies Act is changed to give LRFs more responsibility, funding must follow and boundaries should be aligned so partners can coordinate without mapping headaches.

chapters.title: Education, business and digital risks
chapters.takeaway: Teaching resilience in schools, engaging businesses as partners, and planning for digital failures are vital next steps.

turns.speaker: Helen Maguire
turns.text: What's the role of schools and companies in a whole‑of‑society approach?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: I'd like resilience on the curriculum. Programs like Crucial Crew for primary children work well but are inconsistent across LRFs; children tell their families and spread the message.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Education builds civic capacity; FE and universities teach the technical skills we'll need. Business funds much of recovery and can create accessible resilience products and supply‑chain support.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Are you worried about dependence on technology companies and AI for government services?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Yes. Digital optimisation helps but creates single points of failure: if power or networks go down, people need non‑digital backups, and messaging must reach AI‑native groups differently.

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Operationally, my role is dealing with the fallout when systems fail; we build trusted local social channels, identify community leaders and use reputable local radio during incidents.

turns.speaker: Lord Godson
turns.text: Where does misinformation come from locally?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Mostly social media and AI‑generated streams; it isn't usually a single ideological source. Local BBC radio and trusted community pages help counter it with verified information.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Training and twinning with journalists helps: it aligns expectations between those who seek rapid answers and responders who must stabilise and investigate before drawing conclusions.

chapters.title: Exercises, leadership and governance
chapters.takeaway: Local exercises, strong operational leadership, clear political accountability and matched funding improve crisis response.

turns.speaker: Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom
turns.text: Would public exercises help, and how do we engage apathetic people?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Exercises are valuable for people who want to engage. We do rest‑centre training and invite community volunteers, but we wouldn't force everyone to take part.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Exercising changes mindsets and builds trust; it is best done locally and tailored to the community instead of a single national drill that would be costly and distant from local needs.

turns.speaker: Lord Tunnicliffe
turns.text: Do we have people who can make quick operational decisions in crises, and do they need special training?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Yes—strong leadership is essential. The UK Resilience Academy offers management courses; we debrief after incidents to spot who needs development and to strengthen roles.

turns.speaker: Lord Jack of Courance
turns.text: On devolved administrations: should we seek common rules for borderless threats like viruses?

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: From a crisis management view, coordinated action across administrations reduces confusion, though the political arrangements are a separate question.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are mayoralties effective for resilience?

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Mayor‑led resilience boards can be beneficial if regional footprints and other boundaries align; Northumbria's model shows advantages when the mayor chairs a resilience board.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Mayors bring political accountability and resources, but need specialist resilience expertise beneath them; shared competence and clarity on responsibilities are critical.

chapters.title: Conclusions and priorities
chapters.takeaway: Keep the 'Be Ready' baseline, but follow up with funding, clear local communications, incentives for households and better digital planning.

turns.speaker: Professor Lee Miles
turns.text: Summing up: four priorities—explain context so people understand cascades of risk; empower choices; enable actions with incentives and products; evaluate results to learn what works.

turns.speaker: Becky Heginbotham-Blount
turns.text: Practically: standardise messaging, fund LRFs and partners properly, publicise the local brand (like 'Suffolk Prepared'), involve MPs and community leaders, and keep exercising and learning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. Your evidence shows the campaign is a useful start but must be backed by funding, local clarity, incentives for households and better digital planning.
